notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 1 Chronicles 2:1–28, drawn from the sources listed above. I have noted where specific traditions could not be found in the available material.

---

# 1 Chronicles 2:1–28 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

## vv. 1–2 — The Twelve Sons of Israel

**Traditional Reading:**

The Chronicler opens the genealogies of “all Israel” with the twelve sons of Jacob (Israel), establishing the covenant nation before narrowing to the tribe of Judah. The list closely follows Genesis 35:23–26, but with one notable difference: Dan appears *before* Joseph and Benjamin rather than after them (as in Genesis).

- **Ellicott:** The Chronicler omits the mothers and moves Dan forward, “as if to hint that Dan was considered Rachel’s elder son” (cf. Genesis 30:6). He notes that accident may have caused the transposition. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-1.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The order is: (1) the six sons of Leah; (2) the elder son of Rachel’s handmaid Bilhah (Dan); (3) the two sons of Rachel; (4) the remaining son of Bilhah (Naphtali); (5) the two sons of Zilpah. Because this order “corresponds with nothing in our Old Testament, it may serve as one slight indication that the compiler of Chronicles was not dependent on these records alone.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-2.html)

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The different placement of Dan “is perhaps to be accounted for by Rachel’s wishing the son of her maid Bilhah to be accounted her own” (Genesis 30:3–6). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-1.htm)

- **Barnes’ Notes:** If Dan were moved after Benjamin, the order would reflect legitimacy: Leah’s six sons, Rachel’s two, Bilhah’s two, Zilpah’s two. Dan’s prominence may be explained by his occupying the seventh place in Jacob’s blessing (Genesis 49:16). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-1.htm)

- **Gill:** The first four names (Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah) come from Leah in birth order; then Issachar and Zebulun (also Leah); between Dan and Naphtali (sons of Bilhah) are placed Joseph and Benjamin (sons of Rachel). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-1.htm)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** These twelve sons became thirteen tribes because two tribes came from Joseph (Manasseh and Ephraim). The line of the patriarchs began with Abraham, passed to Isaac (not Ishmael), then to Jacob/Israel (not Esau); but with the twelve sons, all were chosen as covenant inheritors. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

- **Precept Austin:** Chronicles gives special attention to Judah because the book focuses on the Davidic kingdom and God’s covenant promises to David’s line. The genealogies served to preserve tribal identity after the exile, establish inheritance rights, and trace the messianic lineage. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-2-commentary)

**NET Bible notes:** The groupings and conjunctions reflect the Hebrew text’s structure. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Ch+2%3A1-15)

---

## v. 3 — The Three Sons of Judah by Bath-shua; Er’s Death

**Traditional Reading:**

Judah’s genealogy is taken up first, though he was the fourth son, because the Davidic dynasty and the Messiah spring from him. The three sons by Bath-shua (daughter of Shua the Canaanite) are named: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er was “wicked in the sight of the LORD” and the LORD put him to death — quoted nearly verbatim from Genesis 38:7.

- **Ellicott:** “Suppressing other details relating to the sons of Judah, the chronicler copies this statement intact from Genesis, because it thoroughly harmonises with the moral he wishes to be drawn from the entire history of his people.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

- **Benson:** Judah is placed first because the dominion was conferred on him (Genesis 49:8); his tribe held pre-eminence even before David, and “the chief reason … is because the Messiah was to descend from him.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

- **Gill:** The genealogy begins with Judah “not only because Jesse and David sprang from him, but also the King Messiah.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

- **Poole:** Judah is first because the best part of the firstborn’s right — dominion — was conferred on him, and because the Messiah was to come from his loins. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

- **Precept Austin (J.A. Thompson):** “From a genealogical perspective, the royal clan of Judah did not show much promise. His eldest son Er died because of wickedness. … It was rather through the sordid incident of Judah and his daughter-in-law Tamar … that the promised heritage was perpetuated.” The text shows both “the consequences of sin (death of Er) and also the grace of God abounding in the midst of it.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-2-commentary)

**NET Bible notes:** “Bathshua” means “daughter of Shua”; Shua is identified in Genesis 38:2 as a “Canaanite man.” (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Ch+2%3A1-15)

---

## v. 4 — Tamar, Perez, and Zerah

**Traditional Reading:**

Judah’s daughter-in-law Tamar bore him the twins Perez and Zerah, bringing Judah’s total sons to five. The verse alludes to the events of Genesis 38 — Tamar’s disguise as a prostitute, Judah’s failure to provide Shelah as a husband, and his confession that “she is more righteous than I.”

- **Precept Austin:** Perez became especially important because the messianic line runs through him: “Perez → Hezron → Ram … → David → Jesus Christ (Ruth 4:18–22; Matthew 1:3).” The verse demonstrates that “God’s purposes continue despite human failure and moral weakness” and that “God often works through unexpected people and circumstances.” Matthew deliberately includes Tamar in Jesus’ genealogy, “showing that the grace of God reaches into scandal, shame, and human failure.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-2-commentary)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Septuagint in Genesis 38:2 inaccurately gives Shua as the daughter’s name (Σαυά) rather than the father’s. Er and Onan died without issue; Shelah’s descendants appear only in 1 Chronicles 4:21–23. The line is carried on through the twin sons of Tamar. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This genealogy deliberately includes figures with darker testimonies — Er, Onan, Tamar — showing that “God’s covenantal line continued despite the presence of sin and disobedience.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

**NET Bible notes:** No extra comment beyond the translation. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Ch+2%3A1-15)

---

## v. 5 — The Sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul

**Traditional Reading:**

These two names are drawn from Genesis 46:12 and Numbers 26:21. Hezron becomes the crucial link through whom the Davidic line descends. Hamul is listed but never figures prominently in the biblical narrative.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** These two sons of Pharez (Perez) are from Genesis 46:12 and Ruth 4:18. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

- **Ellicott:** Simply notes the continuity with Genesis 46:12. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

---

## v. 6 — The Five Sons of Zerah

**Traditional Reading:**

Zerah (Zara in Matthew 1:3) had five sons: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara (or Darda). These names are otherwise unknown outside this passage, unless they are the same as the “sons of Mahol” mentioned in 1 Kings 4:31.

- **Barnes’ Notes:** “Here, for the first time, the writer of Chronicles draws from sources not otherwise known to us, recording facts not mentioned in the earlier Scriptures.” Barnes argues there are “no sufficient grounds for identifying them with the ‘sons of Mahol’” of 1 Kings 4:31. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-chronicles-2.html)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The weight of evidence favours identifying these four names with those of 1 Kings 4:31, famed for their wisdom. If they are *not* identical, “this very passage proves that the compiler drew on resources not possessed by us.” Many Hebrew manuscripts, plus the Targum, Syriac, and Arabic versions, read “Darda” rather than “Dara.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

- **NET Bible notes:** Many medieval Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read “Darda” (see 1 Kings 4:31). (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Ch+2%3A1-15)

---

## v. 7 — The Son of Carmi: Achar (Achan)

**Traditional Reading:**

Achar (Achan in Joshua 7) is called “the troubler of Israel” for violating the ban on devoted things (the *ḥērem*). His name is changed slightly from “Achan” to “Achar” to resemble the Hebrew word for “troubler” (*ʿākar*).

- **Barnes’ Notes:** “Achan (Joshua 7:1) seems to have become ‘Achar,’ in order to assimilate the word more closely to the Hebrew term for ‘troubler,’ which was from the time of Achan’s sin regarded as the true meaning of his name.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-chronicles-2.html)

- **Bullinger:** The plural “sons” is put for “son” by the figure of speech synecdoche. “Transgressed” is Hebrew *maʿal* (unfaithfulness). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/1-chronicles-2.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Selman):** “Achan was also guilty of ‘unfaithfulness,’ a key term in Chronicles. … This word has the nuance of depriving God of his due, and is Chronicles’ favourite explanation for the disaster of the exile.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

- **Pulpit Commentary (J.R. Thomson):** Achan was a transgressor. Covetousness, temptation, and the yielding of the will all played their part. “Practical lessons: 1. Before transgression, ‘Be sure your sin will find you out.’ 2. After transgression, the trouble that comes upon the sinner is sent in mercy. 3. Confession and repentance, and faith in Christ, are necessary in order to reconciliation and acceptance.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-2.html)

- **NET Bible notes:** “Achar” means “disaster”; a few medieval Hebrew manuscripts read “Achan.” The description is “the troubler of Israel who was unfaithful with respect to the devoted [things].” (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Ch+2%3A1-15)

---

## v. 8 — The Son of Ethan: Azariah

**Traditional Reading:**

A brief note that Azariah was the son of Ethan (one of Zerah’s five sons). No further detail is given anywhere in Scripture about this Azariah.

- No commentator in the consulted sources expands on this verse beyond stating the fact. The Pulpit Commentary treats it as part of the Zerahite genealogy.

---

## v. 9 — The Three Sons of Hezron: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb (Chelubai)

**Traditional Reading:**

Hezron, son of Perez, is the pivotal figure whose three sons branch into three major family lines: Jerahmeel (the firstborn), Ram (ancestor of David), and Chelubai (Caleb). The Chronicler treats these three lines in reverse order — Ram first (vv. 10–17), then Caleb/Chelubai (vv. 18–24), then Jerahmeel (vv. 25–41).

- **Ellicott:** “Chelubai — Strictly, the Chelubite or Calebite, a gentilic term formed from Caleb (1 Chronicles 2:18). This seems to show that we are concerned here not so much with individual sons of Hezron as with families or clans of Hezronites.” Ram is called “Aram” in Matthew 1:3–4; both names mean “high” and are used interchangeably. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-9.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The three lines are treated in reverse order — Ram first because David descends from him; then Chelubai/Caleb from whose line came the illustrious Bezalel; finally Jerahmeel, the firstborn. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-9.htm)

- **Gill:** Chelubai is “afterwards called Caleb.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-9.htm)

- **NET Bible notes:** The Hebrew text has “Celubai,” but see v. 18 where Caleb is described as the son of Hezron. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Ch+2%3A1-15)

---

## vv. 10–12 — Ram to Jesse: The Davidic Line

**Traditional Reading:**

These three verses trace the direct royal line through ten generations: Ram → Amminadab → Nahshon → Salmon (Salma) → Boaz → Obed → Jesse. This matches Ruth 4:18–22 and Matthew 1:3–5.

- **Pulpit Commentary / Preacher’s Complete Homiletical:** Nahshon was the “prince of the children of Judah” (Numbers 2:3) at the Exodus. The five names from Salma to David “cover a period of at least 450 years from the Exodus to the birth of Solomon.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-chronicles-2.html)

- **Gill:** Ram is mentioned in the genealogy of Christ in Matthew 1:3–4, where he is called Aram. Nahshon was the leader of Judah when Israel came out of Egypt and camped under their standards (Numbers 2:3). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-9.htm)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This section “deals with the line of Judah to David, the founder of the Davidic dynasty that ruled over Israel and Judah.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

- **NET Bible notes:** The LXX reads “Salmon” (cf. Ruth 4:21). (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=1Ch+2%3A1-15)

---

## vv. 13–15 — The Seven Sons of Jesse, David the Seventh

**Traditional Reading:**

Jesse had eight sons (1 Samuel 16:10–11; 17:12), but only seven are named here: Eliab, Abinadab, Shimea, Nethanel, Raddai, Ozem, and David (the seventh/youngest). The eighth son is not named in Chronicles.

- **Bullinger:** “Jesse begat eight sons (1 Samuel 16:5–11 and 1 Chronicles 17:12–14). Here seven are numbered and named, and David is the seventh and the youngest; the eighth may have died young and left no issue. While it was proper to mention the eight in the history, it is unnecessary to do so in the genealogy.” Bullinger also notes that the different spelling of many names in Chronicles (with vowels written in full) “shows an independent origin.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/1-chronicles-2.html)

- **Barnes’ Notes:** “Jesse had eight sons, of whom David was the youngest … Probably one of the sons shown to Samuel at Bethlehem did not grow up.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/1-chronicles-2.html)

---

## vv. 16–17 — The Sisters of David: Zeruiah and Abigail

**Traditional Reading:**

David’s sisters (or half-sisters) were Zeruiah and Abigail. Zeruiah’s three sons — Abishai, Joab, and Asahel — became David’s famous warriors. Abigail’s son was Amasa, whose father was Jether (or Ithra) the Ishmaelite.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Payne):** “The genealogies of these four warriors, made famous under their half-uncle David (cf. 2 Samuel 2:18–19; 19:13), are not drawn from 2 Samuel … but apart from this later passage, we would not have known that their mothers, Zeruiah and Abigail, were step-daughters of Jesse, born to David’s mother by her presumably earlier marriage to Nahash.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

- **Bullinger:** Zeruiah is called “sister of David.” Nahash (2 Samuel 17:25) may have been the father of Jesse’s wife; thus Zeruiah and Abigail were half-sisters of David. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/1-chronicles-2.html)

---

## v. 18 — Caleb Son of Hezron: Wife Azubah and Jerioth

**Traditional Reading:**

This Caleb is distinct from the more famous Caleb son of Jephunneh (the faithful spy). The verse introduces the family of Caleb son of Hezron, with his wife Azubah and (possibly a second wife or concubine) Jerioth. The sons of Azubah were Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik, citing Selman):** “In practice, the otherwise unknown Caleb son of Hezron is probably distinct from Caleb, a Kenizzite and son of Jephunneh, who is frequently said to have ‘followed the LORD wholeheartedly’ (e.g. Numbers 14:24; 32:12; Joshua 14:6, 13–14).” Caleb the Kenizzite is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:15–16. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

- The Pulpit Commentary treats this section as the line of Chelubai/Caleb, one of the three branches of Hezron.

---

## vv. 19–20 — Caleb Marries Ephrath; Hur, Uri, Bezalel

**Traditional Reading:**

After Azubah’s death, Caleb married Ephrath (or Ephrathah), who bore Hur. Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezalel — the master craftsman of the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1–5).

- This is a significant note: the Chronicler traces the descent of Bezalel, the Spirit-filled artisan who built the tabernacle furnishings, through this side-line of Judah.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** These obscure names connected with Judah are listed because most returning exiles were from Judah and Benjamin (cf. Ezra 1:5; 10:9). The genealogies connected the post-exilic community to their pre-exilic tribal inheritance and land claims. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

---

## vv. 21–23 — Hezron and the Daughter of Machir; Segub, Jair, Havvoth-jair

**Traditional Reading:**

Later, Hezron (now advanced in age, at sixty) married the daughter of Machir, the “father of Gilead” — a prominent Manassite. She bore Segub, who fathered Jair. Jair possessed twenty-three cities in Gilead (called Havvoth-jair, “towns of Jair”). But Geshur and Aram (Syria) captured these towns along with Kenath and its sixty villages. The passage notes that all these belonged to the descendants of Machir.

- This section connects Judah’s genealogy with the Transjordanian territory of Manasseh, showing inter-tribal links through marriage.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This is a side-line in Judah that intertwined with the family of Machir of Manasseh. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

- No other commentator in the sources consulted expands significantly on these verses.

---

## v. 24 — Hezron’s Death and Posthumous Son: Ashhur

**Traditional Reading:**

After Hezron died in Caleb-ephrathah (likely Bethlehem, associated with the clan of Caleb), his wife Abijah bore him a posthumous son, Ashhur, who became the “father” (founder) of Tekoa — a town in Judah, later the home of the prophet Amos.

- **Pulpit Commentary (Clarkson):** Notes the human variety in family life: here “a child born after its father’s death.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-2.html)

---

## vv. 25–26 — The Sons of Jerahmeel, Firstborn of Hezron

**Traditional Reading:**

The Chronicler now traces the line of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron. His sons by his first wife: Ram (the firstborn — not to be confused with Ram in v. 10), Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. Jerahmeel had another wife, Atarah, who was the mother of Onam.

- **Gill and Ellicott** note that this Ram is a different Ram from the one who fathered Amminadab in the Davidic line (v. 10). The names overlap, which is a common feature of biblical genealogies.

---

## vv. 27–28 — Ram (Firstborn of Jerahmeel) and Onam

**Traditional Reading:**

v. 27: The sons of Ram (firstborn of Jerahmeel) were Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.

v. 28: The sons of Onam (son of Jerahmeel by Atarah) were Shammai and Jada. The verse ends mid-sentence: “The sons of Shammai:” — which continues in v. 29 with Nadab and Abishur.

- These names are otherwise unknown in Scripture. They represent the Jerahmeelite clan of Judah, whose inclusion demonstrates the Chronicler’s concern for completeness and for connecting the post-exilic community to all branches of the tribe.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** “This traces a side-line in the tribe of Judah, separate from the line that culminated in David.” The list of side-lines “show[s] how diverse the tribe of Judah was, even as it climaxed in the line leading to David.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences

**Across Protestant traditions (Reformed, Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Lutheran):** The consulted sources do not reveal significant *doctrinal* disagreements on this genealogical chapter. All mainstream traditions read it as a historical record establishing the Davidic and messianic line. The main differences are in *emphasis*:

- **Reformed / Presbyterian** sources (via Selman, cited by Guzik) emphasize God’s sovereign covenant faithfulness through flawed human instruments, and the Chronicler’s theological message that “unfaithfulness” (*maʿal*) explains the exile. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

- **Baptist / Evangelical** sources (Gill, Precept Austin) draw strong attention to Christ in the genealogy: “not only because Jesse and David sprang from him, but also the King Messiah.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/2-3.htm)

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic** (Enduring Word): David Guzik applies the genealogy to the believer’s life — God works through “ordinary, imperfect people” and genealogy reminds us that “God’s purposes continue despite human failure.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-2/)

- **Lutheran and Anglican** sources were not specifically identified among the consulted pages for this passage.

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** No results were returned from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for this specific passage. The Pulpit Commentary (an older Anglican/Protestant work) was the closest to a broader church tradition consulted.

**Modern Scholarship:** The NET Bible notes provide text-critical observations (e.g., “Darda” vs. “Dara,” “Achar” vs. “Achan,” “Salmon” vs. “Salma”) but do not fundamentally reinterpret the passage. Barnes’ Notes (19th century) observes that the Chronicler “draws from sources not otherwise known to us.” Bibleodyssey.org was not reached in the search results.

**Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace:** No specific teaching on this passage from these movements was found in the available sources.
